content: Please read the README.md assignment description, including the grading rubric. Tell me what I need to do and what I need to understand in order to complete the assignment.

I read the README and the starter project. The deadline is September 22, 2026 at 11:59 PM CT, so deployment should not be left until the end.

The assignment is to create a single-page scrolling website on any topic using HTML5, SCSS, and vanilla JavaScript. Libraries and frameworks such as Bootstrap, jQuery, React, and UIKit are not allowed. Inline styles, inline scripts, and HTML tables used for layout are also prohibited. Sources must be declared.

The sixteen required features are:

1. A full-width single-page layout with a header, horizontal sections, and a footer.
2. A sticky navigation bar.
3. A position indicator that highlights the current section, including the last item at the bottom of the page.
4. A navigation bar that becomes shorter and uses smaller text after scrolling.
5. Smooth scrolling between sections.
6. A carousel with at least three slides and left/right arrows.
7. A layout with at least three columns.
8. Horizontal centering throughout and at least one responsively vertically centered element.
9. A responsive layout at 1920x1080, 1366x768, 1280x720, 1024x768, and 768x1024.
10. A fixed-position background image.
11. A modal window with additional content.
12. An embedded HTML5 video.
13. SCSS features such as variables, mixins, and nesting.
14. CSS3 animation or transitions.
15. Scalable vector icons.
16. Social-media icons.

The largest grading categories are overall design (20%), code quality (12%), smooth scrolling (10%), carousel (10%), modal (10%), and responsiveness (10%). The position indicator, navbar resizing, multi-column layout, and animations are also important. The smaller one- and two-percent items are easy points and should not be omitted.

The starter project is already configured with webpack. The main files are `src/index.html`, `src/css/main.scss`, and `src/js/main.js`; `src/index.js` imports them. Assets belong in `src/assets/`. The main background knowledge needed is semantic HTML, Flexbox/Grid, fixed positioning, media queries, SCSS variables and mixins, DOM event handling, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `classList`, `scrollIntoView()`, transitions, and keyframe animation.

Submission requires a public GitHub Pages deployment, a demonstration video no longer than three minutes, and the grading form. Because an LLM is being used, the chat log and the LLM survey responses are also required under the course policy.

My recommended order is: build the HTML structure, implement the navigation and scrolling behaviors, add the carousel and modal, then refine the visual system and test all five viewport sizes.

The navbar can satisfy sticky positioning, resizing, position indication, and smooth scrolling as one coherent component. SCSS, responsiveness, and horizontal centering apply across the entire page.

The highest-risk details are the bottom-of-page position indicator, the 768x1024 portrait layout, and visual consistency. A special bottom check is usually needed because the final section may never reach the navbar's lower edge. The navigation must also remain usable at 768 pixels wide.

Please list the rules for me.

The README lists seven rules:

1. This is an individual assignment; collaboration is not permitted.
2. Code written by someone else may not be copied and pasted. Sources used for inspiration or clarification must be declared.
3. Libraries such as Bootstrap, jQuery, React, and UIKit are not permitted. The interactions must use vanilla JavaScript.
4. Inline styling is not permitted.
5. Inline script tags are not permitted.
6. HTML tables may not be used for layout.
7. Questions about acceptable approaches should be asked on Piazza.

Font Awesome's CSS icon font and Google Fonts are reasonable boundary cases because the rubric explicitly requests scalable icons and encourages web fonts. The JavaScript Font Awesome kit should be avoided.

The LLM policy also requires the chat log and survey answers. The repository must be public for the expected GitHub Pages workflow. The demonstration video must be at most three minutes, show the deployed URL, and be shared with the course address.

For the concept page, asset sources should be traceable and declared. A footer disclaimer such as `Concept design — not affiliated with Apple Inc.` can clarify that this is not an official product page.
Instead of using photos from the official site, we could just take other people's photos from Google.

Using arbitrary Google Images results creates two practical problems. First, mixed resolutions, color treatments, backgrounds, and watermarks can weaken the 20% design category. Second, Google is a search engine rather than the original source, so every image would still need its actual source and usage rights recorded.

Faster and safer options include Unsplash, Pexels, and Pixabay. If Google Images is used, the search should at least be filtered to Creative Commons licenses and the original source should be recorded. Because the iPhone Duo is fictional, an original CSS device mockup or a mockup generator would also make the concept more internally consistent.

My recommendation is to use a small set of visually consistent, properly licensed technology images for backgrounds while creating the concept device itself as an original CSS element.
Let's change the theme to iPhone 18. I placed several videos and images in the assets folder. Tell me if more are needed, and then continue according to the TODO list.

I inspected the supplied assets. They were Pexels files, including five useful images and two portrait videos. The material was sufficient, and its strongest common visual direction was a dark background with a red accent.

The asset plan was:

| Asset | Use |
|---|---|
| Red-lit phone close-up | Hero background |
| Two phones against the sky | Fixed-background section |
| Three additional phone images | Carousel slides |
| Eight-second red unboxing video | Main Film section |
| Short phone-use video | Looping screen inside the CSS phone mockup |

I compressed and renamed the assets because the original files were unnecessarily large for GitHub Pages. The total asset size was reduced from 13.7 MB to about 1.6 MB. I then built the semantic HTML structure, separated the SCSS into variables, mixins, and main styles, and implemented the interactions in vanilla JavaScript.

The production build initially contained duplicate asset copies because CopyPlugin and webpack's HTML/CSS loaders were both emitting them. Removing the redundant plugin reduced the build from about 3.5 MB to 1.9 MB.

I tested the result in a browser and corrected the parallax overlay contrast, an inaccurate video-duration label, and the phone mockup's vertical position. All five required viewport sizes had zero horizontal overflow. The final implementation included all sixteen rubric items: seven full-width sections, a fixed navbar, a bottom-safe position indicator, navbar resizing, smooth scrolling, a three-slide carousel with arrows/dots/keyboard control, responsive grids, centered hero and modal content, a fixed background, three modals, two HTML5 videos, SCSS variables and mixins, five keyframe animations, Font Awesome icons, and social icons.

The source also passed the rule checks: no inline styles in the HTML, no inline scripts, no table-based layout, and no runtime framework. Remaining tasks were deployment, the LLM log, and the demonstration video.

The phone body is not an image. It is a CSS-styled element, and the video acts as its screen. Padding around the video exposes the phone's metallic frame. The structure is: ```html
``` The frame uses a three-stop linear gradient for a metallic reflection, `padding: 10px` for the bezel, and a 44px outer radius. Its width is `min(250px, 70vw)` and `aspect-ratio: 9 / 19.5`, so it scales without distortion. The screen radius is 34px: outer radius minus the 10px padding, which keeps the inner and outer curves visually concentric. The screen uses `width: 100%`, `height: 100%`, `object-fit: cover`, and `display: block`. `object-fit` crops the 9:16 source to the taller screen without stretching it; block display removes the baseline gap of an inline media element. The Dynamic Island is absolutely positioned above the video and centered with `left: 50%` plus `translateX(-50%)`. The video attributes have separate purposes: `muted` permits autoplay, `autoplay` starts it, `loop` restarts the short clip, and `playsinline` prevents forced full-screen playback on iOS. There are no controls because this is decorative content. By contrast, the Film video carries content and waits for hover, focus, or click through JavaScript. [tools used: Bash]
I understand now. Please perform a self-check to see whether any requirement is still missing.

I performed a browser-based audit. The first modal-overlay test clicked the center of the overlay, where the dialog correctly intercepted the click, so I corrected the test to click a visible corner of the backdrop.

The audit passed all sixteen requirements. Evidence included eight full-width page regions; a fixed navbar remaining at `top: 0` after scrolling; every linked section activating in turn; `Order` activating at the bottom; navbar height changing from 91px to 59px, link text from 17px to 14px, and brand text from 24px to 18px; smooth scrolling; a three-slide looping carousel with side arrows and dots; responsive three-, two-, and one-column grids; hero centering at multiple viewport heights; zero horizontal overflow or clipped text in all five required resolutions; a fixed background; three accessible modals closing by button, backdrop, or Escape; two HTML5 videos; extensive SCSS variables/mixins; five custom keyframe animations; thirty rendered Font Awesome icons; and five social icons.

The only failed request was a missing favicon, so I added a small SVG favicon. A crude overflow diagnostic initially reported eleven elements, but all were inactive carousel slides intentionally clipped by the carousel viewport.

The HTML source contains no inline styles. At runtime, two values are assigned through JavaScript: the carousel track transform and the continuous reading-progress width. My judgment was that the rule prohibits style declarations embedded in the HTML source; these runtime values are interaction state implemented in the external JavaScript file. Rewriting the carousel at the deadline would add compatibility risk without improving compliance meaningfully.

The code portion was complete. Remaining work was deployment, the LLM log, and the submission video.

I checked the repository and workflow first. Two issues needed correction: `build/` should be ignored because CI creates it, and the pattern `assets/` was unintentionally ignoring `src/assets/` as well as the root folder. I changed the latter to `/assets/` so the optimized media files would be committed. I also confirmed that built resource paths were relative and compatible with the `/mp1/` GitHub Pages subdirectory.

Deployment steps:

1. Create a public `mp1` repository under the student's GitHub account without adding another README, `.gitignore`, or license.
2. Change the local `origin` from the course template to the new repository:

```bash
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<username>/mp1.git
git remote -v
```

3. Commit and push:

```bash
git add -A
git status
git commit -m "Build iPhone 18 concept page for MP1"
git push -u origin main
```

4. In repository Settings, open Pages and select `GitHub Actions` as the Build and deployment source.
5. Wait for the `Deploy static content to Pages` workflow to finish successfully.
6. Open `https://<username>.github.io/mp1/` and verify the hero image, all gallery images, both videos, the Inter font, and Font Awesome icons.

Future changes deploy automatically after another commit and push.
